headline: 3 A.M. at the Gut: One Cast, One 34-Pound Bass, and a Sound Building Toward Something
subhead: The current's loading up for the new moon and the first signs of albie water are creeping toward The Race — here's what's actually biting right now.
body_markdown:
Three-fifteen Wednesday morning, standing on the rocks at Plum Gut with the tide just turning to ebb, I put a Gibbs Danny plug on the seam where the fast water meets the slick behind the boulder pile. Third cast, the plug got walloped so hard I thought I'd hung a mooring. Thirty-four pounds of striper, hooked in six feet of white water, released in under ninety seconds because I wasn't about to stretch that fight in current that strong. That's the kind of bite the Gut gives up right now — not volume, but quality, and only if you're willing to fish it in the dark on the moving water.

That's the pattern across the eastern end right now: deep, current-driven, mostly nocturnal. We flagged this two weeks back — said the deep/night bass pattern would hold until either a cooling trend or the new moon stirred the pot, and that's exactly what's happening. New London's reading 69.4 degrees, which is soft compared to the mid-70s piling up in the western Sound, and that gradient is exactly why the biggest fish out here are still holding deep on structure and current edges instead of chasing bait up on the flats during daylight. The Race is fishing the same way — big bass stacking in the eddies off the lighthouse rock pile on the last two hours of the ebb, plastic eels and 2-ounce bucktails bounced tight to bottom in 25 to 40 feet, and you want to be there before first light because once the sun's up over Fishers Island, the bite shuts like a door.

Bluefish are the better daytime story right now. That resurgence that's been building through the western Sound over deep reef structure has pushed east — I had a solid pick of 4- to 8-pound blues off Fishers Island Wednesday afternoon, working bunker chunks and diamond jigs in 30 feet off the north side, current still running hard enough that you needed a jig heavy enough to hold bottom without babysitting it. Nothing gator-sized yet out here, but the size is trending up week over week, and if the pattern that hit Sandy Hook keeps marching this direction, don't be shocked if we see real teeth on the beach by Labor Day.

Porgies are the bread and butter right now and they're not messing around. Structure fishing off Orient Point and the rock piles around Plum Gut is stacking porgies to 2 pounds on sea worms and squid strips, high-low rigs, size 4 hooks, fished right on the bottom on the slower stages of the tide when the current lets you actually hold in one spot. This has been the most consistent bite in the zone for three weeks running — not glamorous, but if you want fish in the cooler, this is where you get them without burning gas or sleep.

Blackfish scouting is underway too, early but real. I've been marking fish on the sonar around the rock piles off Fishers Island and the reef structure south of Plum Gut, green crab drops producing a few undersized tog already. Too early to target them seriously — season's not open and the bite's not dialed in yet — but the presence is there, and that's worth banking for when the fall pattern kicks in.

Here's the part that matters most for the next 72 hours: the new moon on the 12th is loading the tidal range fast, and that's the same mechanism that's been pushing bonito out of Rhode Island through Watch Hill and Sakonnet toward Buzzards Bay. We called this zone as an early beneficiary of that push back on August 3rd, said the eastern Sound sits close enough to open water off The Race to catch spillover if albies or bonito start showing before the new moon peak — and the corridor's still building in that direction. Nothing confirmed yet inside The Race or Plum Gut itself, but the warm current extension is real and this is exactly the kind of setup — building tide, warming edge water, bait pushed tight to structure — that flips the switch fast once it starts.

If I had one trip to make this week, I'd fish the last two hours of the ebb at the Gut before sunrise for bass, then slide over to the Fishers Island rock piles midday for blues and porgy, and I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small epoxy jig in the rocket launcher just in case something with a forked tail shows up chasing bait on the surface. That's not a guarantee — it's a bet based on where the water's heading. The tide's building, the temperature gradient is sharpening the bass bite into a tight window, and the corridor that feeds albies into this end of the Sound is getting more current and warmer water by the day. Worth being out there when it flips.
